poi.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
poi.short_description: Gothic cathedral on Ile de la Cite whose construction began in 1163, reopened after restoration following the 2019 fire

beats.script_body: Notre-Dame endured centuries of vandalism before the Revolution even began. The medieval chancel screen was destroyed in 1699 to make way for a more fashionable baroque interior. The original stained glass windows — except for the three great rose windows — were ripped out and replaced with plain white glass to 'let in more light.'

Eugene Viollet-le-Duc began his controversial restoration of Notre-Dame in 1844, guided by his famous principle: 'To restore a building is not to maintain it, repair it, or rebuild it; it is to re-establish it in a complete state which may never have existed at any given moment.' He added the spire, the gargoyles, and much of what the world came to think of as 'original' medieval decoration.

In Rabelais's tale, the giant Gargantua visited Notre-Dame and, followed and gawked at by Parisians, climbed the church tower and urinated on the crowd below, drowning 260,418 people (exclusive of women and children). In Rabelais's version, the city of Lutetia became known as Paris — from 'par rie' (for a laugh) — in recognition of Gargantua's jest.

Victor Hugo's 1831 novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame was written partly as a plea to save the crumbling cathedral. The book ignited a wave of public passion for the medieval monument and directly led to the campaign for its restoration — proof that a novel can save a building.

Notre-Dame hosted only two coronations, both controversial: Henry VI of England, who had conquered France, and Emperor Napoleon. The legitimate French dynasties always used the cathedral of Reims. Henri IV's conversion to Catholicism was celebrated here in 1593 with a Te Deum, though the conversion ceremony itself took place at Saint-Denis.

Notre-Dame was the birthplace of polyphonic music in Europe. In the 12th and 13th centuries, the composers Leonin and Perotin developed the art of organum — music in multiple voices — at the cathedral's choir school. Their innovations laid the foundations for all Western harmony.

Beneath Notre-Dame's chancel, vestiges of a pillar-shaped monument dedicated to Jupiter were found in 1711 — the Pilier des Nautes, erected by the corporation of water merchants (Nautae Parisiaci). Inscriptions date it to the reign of Emperor Tiberius (AD 14-37), making it the oldest sculpted monument found in the capital. The merchants engraved their own gods alongside those of Rome. The pillar is now displayed in the Musee National du Moyen Age at the Hotel de Cluny.

Notre-Dame's great bell, known today as Emmanuel, has a dramatic history. The original bell, called Jacqueline, was recast in 1680 and renamed Emmanuel. According to tradition, the ladies of the court threw their jewellery into the molten metal, which is said to give the bell its exceptionally pure tone.

During the Paris Commune in May 1871, Communards attempted to burn Notre-Dame by piling chairs and furniture against the doors and setting them alight. Doctors and staff from the neighbouring Hotel-Dieu rushed across and extinguished the flames, saving the cathedral from destruction.

The 28 statues of the Kings of Judah on the west facade were torn down by Revolutionaries who mistook them for the Kings of France. The heads were discovered in 1977 during construction work near the Opera and are now displayed at the Musee de Cluny.

Between 1163 and 1330, anonymous artisans carved Notre-Dame from stone, slipping imperceptibly from the Romanesque to the Gothic style yet sustaining architectural unity. Bishop Maurice de Sully initiated the project, commissioning a monument to transcend every other in the kingdom.

During the Revolution, Notre-Dame was nearly lost forever. Stripped of its treasures and rededicated to the Cult of Reason, it was put up for sale as building material. A certain Citoyen Simon nearly purchased the cathedral — one of the closest brushes with destruction in the building's history.

poi.name: Sainte-Chapelle
poi.short_description: 13th-century Gothic royal chapel with 15 stained-glass windows depicting 1,113 biblical scenes across 600 square metres

beats.script_body: The only part of the Ile de la Cite's old palace that remains in its entirety is the Sainte-Chapelle, its fragile-looking spire soaring above the Palais buildings, its excessive height in relation to its length giving it the appearance of a lopped-off cathedral choir. Though damaged in the Revolution — when it was used as a flour warehouse — it was sensitively restored in the mid-nineteenth century, and remains one of the finest achievements of French High Gothic, renowned for its exquisite stained glass. It was built by Louis IX in 1242 to 1248 to house a collection of holy relics bought at an extortionate price — far more than the chapel itself cost — from the bankrupt Byzantine Empire. The relics, supposedly Christ's crown of thorns and fragments of the True Cross and a nail of the crucifixion, are now in Notre-Dame's treasury, displayed only on certain days, including Good Friday.

beats.source_passage: The only part of the Ile de la Cite's old palace that remains in its entirety is the Sainte-Chapelle, its fragile-looking spire soaring above the Palais buildings and its excessive height in relation to its length giving it the appearance of a lopped-off cathedral choir. Though damaged in the Revolution, during which it was used as a flour warehouse, it was sensitively restored in the mid-nineteenth century, and remains one of the finest achievements of French High Gothic, renowned for its exquisite stained-glass windows. It was built by Louis IX in 1242–48 to house a collection of holy relics bought at an extortionate price – far more than it cost to build the Sainte-Chapelle – from the bankrupt Byzantium Empire. The relics, supposedly Christ's crown of thorns and fragments of the True Cross and a nail of the crucifixion, are now in Notre-Dame's treasury, displayed only on certain days, including Good Friday.

beats.script_body: The Sainte-Chapelle actually consists of two chapels: the simple lower chapel was intended for the servants, and the upper chapel, reached via a spiral staircase, was reserved for the court. The upper chapel is dazzling — its walls made almost entirely of stained glass held up by powerful supports that the medieval builders cleverly crafted to appear delicate and fragile by dividing them into clusters of pencil-thin columns. When the sun streams through, the glowing blues and reds of the stained glass dapple the interior and you feel like you're surrounded by myriad brilliant butterflies.

When the sun streams through, the glowing blues and reds of the stained glass dapple the interior and you feel like you're surrounded by myriad brilliant butterflies.

beats.script_body: In 2008, a seven-year, ten-million-euro programme of restoration began. It cleaned and preserved all the stained glass, cleaned the façade stonework, and conserved sculpture. Half the funding came from private donors; the other half from the Villum Foundation. An innovative thermoformed glass layer was added outside the medieval windows for protection. The flamboyant rose window on the west façade was completed in 2015 — in time for the 800th anniversary of the birth of St. Louis.

beats.source_passage: In 2008, a more comprehensive seven-year programme of restoration began, costing some €10 million to clean and preserve all the stained glass, clean the facade stonework and conserve and repair some of the sculptures. Half of the funding was provided by private donors, the other half coming from the Villum Foundation. Included in the restoration was an innovative thermoformed glass layer applied outside the stained-glass windows for added protection. The restoration of the flamboyant rose window on the west facade was completed in 2015 in time for the 800th anniversary of the birth of St. Louis.

beats.script_body: Louis's chapel became a template. As his saintly status grew across European aristocracies, the building's design migrated: Karlštejn Castle near Prague (around 1360), the Hofburgkapelle in Vienna (consecrated 1449), the Collegiate Church of the Holy Cross and St. Bartholomew in Wrocław (around 1350), and even Exeter College, Oxford (1860). Each was a sacred space and a piece of soft diplomacy in one.

Hofburgkapelle in Vienna consecrated 1449
Collegiate Church of the Holy Cross and St Bartholomew, Wrocław (c. 1350)
Exeter College, Oxford (1860)
Such chapels worked as diplomatic tools as well as piety
beats.source_passage:
As the status of Saint Louis grew among Europe's aristocracy, the influence of his famous chapel also extended beyond France, with important copies at Karlštejn Castle near Prague (c. 1360), the Hofburgkapelle in Vienna (consecrated 1449), Collegiate Church of the Holy Cross and St. Bartholomew, Wrocław (c. 1350) and Exeter College, Oxford (1860).
For the patrons, such chapels served not only as public expressions of personal piety but also as valuable diplomatic tools, encouraging important visitors to come and venerate their relics and showing their connection to the French crown.

beats.script_body: The Sainte-Chapelle was built by Saint Louis to house a piece of the Holy Cross and the Crown of Thorns, which he bought from Baudouin II, the last Emperor of Constantinople, who was in desperate need of funds to defend his city. The architects — Pierre de Montreuil, or perhaps Jean de Chelles — were set an unusual brief: design a chapel to have the light, lacy aspect of a reliquary. The result was stunningly beyond expectation. It took barely five years. The silver and gold reliquary that originally held the Crown of Thorns was sent to the Mint during the Revolution, but its contents — genuine or not — miraculously survived and are kept today at Notre-Dame. Even the standard-bearers of the Revolutionary ideal, it seems, did not dare to tamper with the most holy of Christian symbols. The chapel itself was shown no such consideration: it served as a flour store, then as a depot for court archives, growing so dilapidated that in 1847 it still bore an inscription reading 'National property, for sale.' Fortunately enlightened souls called on Viollet-le-Duc, Lassus, and others to restore the church, and 720 of the 1,134 original stained-glass scenes were preserved.
beats.source_passage: the Sainte-Chapelle, built by Saint Louis to house a piece of the Holy Cross and the Crown of Thorns. He had bought them from Baudouin II, the last Emperor of Constantinople, who was in desperate need of funds to defend his city. The chapel was therefore designed to have the light, lacy aspect of a reliquary. The result was stunningly beyond expectation. It took its architect (Pierre de Montreuil or, perhaps, Jean de Chelles) barely five years to build a masterpiece of harmonious proportions [...]. Although the silver and gold reliquary containing the crown of thorns was dispatched to the Mint during the Revolution, its contents (whether genuine or not) have miraculously survived and are now kept at Notre-Dame. Is it that even the standard-bearers of the Revolutionary ideal did not dare to tamper with the most holy of Christian symbols? The chapel was not shown the same consideration and was used first to store flour, then as a depot for the court house archives; by which time it was so dilapidated that it was put on the market for sale and demolition. In 1847 it still bore an inscription which read: 'National property, for sale'. Fortunately, some enlightened souls [...] called upon Viollet-le-Duc, Lassus and other artists to restore the church to its ancient beauty. [...] 720 of the 1,134 original scenes having been preserved.

beats.script_body: A combined ticket can be purchased for visiting both the museum and the Sainte-Chapelle, built in the 1240s. The stained glass windows here are the finest in Paris, being intended for the private chapel of the King. St Louis had the chapel built to house the Crown of Thorns and other precious holy relics that can now be seen in Notre-Dame.

beats.script_body: There are 1,113 glass panels in the upper chapel, two-thirds of them original — the rest date from the nineteenth-century restoration. Together they tell virtually the entire story of the Bible: starting on the north side with Genesis, continuing with the Passion of Christ at the east end and the history of the Sainte-Chapelle relics on the south side, and ending with the Apocalypse in the rose window. The chapel is frequently used for classical concerts; tickets bought a day or so in advance avoid long queues.

beats.script_body: After the Revolution, the Crown of Thorns left Sainte-Chapelle. A new gold and crystal reliquary was made for it, and from the Concordat of 1801 onward it was displayed in the treasury of Notre-Dame. On 15 April 2019, when fire broke out at Notre-Dame, the crown was rescued. It was kept temporarily at the Louvre during the long restoration, and returned to Notre-Dame in December 2024 — eight centuries after Louis carried it barefoot through Paris.

beats.source_passage: During the French Revolution, the Chasse and the vessels holding the relics were taken apart and melted down for their jewels and precious metals. The fragment of the cross was transferred first in 1793 to a collection of antiquities, then given to the Bishop of Paris. A new reliquary of gold and crystal was made for the crown of thorns. Since the Concordat of 1801, it was displayed in the treasury of the cathedral of Notre Dame de Paris, but it was saved from the Notre-Dame de Paris fire on 15 April 2019 and was kept temporarily in the Louvre Museum. It returned to the cathedral in December of 2024.

beats.script_body: The relics arrived in Paris in August 1239, carried from Venice by two Dominican friars. King Louis hosted a week-long celebratory reception. For the final stage of the journey he carried the relics himself, barefoot and dressed as a penitent — a scene shown in the Relics of the Passion window on the south side of the chapel. The numbers reveal what kind of priority this was: Louis paid 135,000 livres for the relics, then a further 100,000 livres for the silver Grand-Chasse to hold them. The chapel itself cost 40,000 livres to build and glaze.

beats.source_passage:
Louis purchased his Passion relics from Baldwin II, the Latin emperor at Constantinople, for the sum of 135,000 livres. This money was paid to the Venetians to whom the relics had been pawned. 
The relics arrived in Paris in August 1239, carried from Venice by two Dominican friars. Upon arrival, King Louis hosted a week-long celebratory reception for the relics. For the final stage of their journey they were carried by Louis IX himself, barefoot and dressed as a penitent, a scene depicted in the Relics of the Passion window on the south side of the chapel. The relics were stored in a large and elaborate silver chest, the Grand-Chasse, on which Louis spent a further 100,000 livres. 
The entire chapel, by contrast, cost 40,000 livres to build and glaze.

beats.script_body: The names of the master glaziers who built these windows between 1242 and 1248 have all been lost. But art historian Louis Grodecki identified three different workshops by style. The first made the apse windows and most of the north wall — supple forms, simplified features. The second, the Master of the Ezekiel Window, made the Ezekiel, Daniel and Kings windows — elongated figures, angular drapery. The third, the Master of Judith and Esther, made those two windows and the window of Job — subtler faces, the feel of an illuminated manuscript.

Louis Grodecki identified three workshops by style

Workshop 2 (Master of Ezekiel): Ezekiel, Daniel, Kings — elongated forms, angular drapery
Workshop 3 (Master of Judith and Esther): plus Job — subtle faces, illuminated-manuscript feel
beats.source_passage: Most of the windows were put into place between 1242 and 1248. The names of the glass artists are unknown, but the art historian Louis Grodecki identified what appear to be three different ateliers with different styles. The windows in the apse and most of the windows on the north wall of the nave are made by one workshop. These works are known for supple forms and costumes, with simplified features. The second workshop, named by Grodecki as Master of the Ezekiel window, made the Ezekiel and Daniel windows, as well as the window of the Kings. That work is characterized by elongated forms, and more elaborate and angular draperies. The third artist or workshop is called the Master of Judith and Esther, for the distinct style of those windows, as well as the window of Job. They are distinguished by more subtle details in the faces, and a resemblance to the figures in illuminated manuscripts.

beats.script_body: On 24 May 1871, barely four years after the full restoration was complete, the Communards poured petrol over the Sainte-Chapelle and only failed to set it on fire for lack of time. Everything you see inside is what they almost burned.
beats.source_passage: on 24 May 1871, barely four years after the completion of the restoration, the Communards had poured petrol over the Sainte-Chapelle, and only failed to set it on fire for lack of time.

beats.script_body: The stained glass was removed and placed in safe storage during World War II. When it was reinstalled in 1945, a layer of external varnish was applied to protect it from the dust and scratches of wartime bombing. Over the decades, that protective varnish gradually darkened, making the already-fading images even harder to see — one of the problems the 2008-2015 restoration would have to solve.

poi.name: Conciergerie
poi.short_description: Medieval royal palace turned Revolutionary prison where Marie Antoinette and over 2,700 inmates were held during the Reign of Terror

beats.script_body: Among the notorious prisoners of the Conciergerie were Ravaillac, the assassin of Henri IV; the mass poisoner La Marquise de Brinvilliers (1630-1676), who had eliminated the better part of her numerous household; and Cartouche (1693-1721), the most notorious bandit of his age and the terror of Paris. To be admitted into Cartouche's prestigious gang, a candidate had to prove himself an expert cutpurse. Candidates were made to practise on dummies covered with little bells until they could strip them clean without the slightest tinkling. All three prisoners awaited execution at the Conciergerie.

Marquise de Brinvilliers mass poisoner 1630-1676
Cartouche notorious bandit 1693-1721 terror of Paris
Gang candidates practised on dummies with bells
beats.source_passage: Candidates were made to practise on dummies covered with little bells, until they could strip them without the slightest tinkling

beats.script_body: At no. 1 quai de l'Horloge stands the entrance to the Conciergerie — originally the seat of the governor of the King's palace, hence its name. It became a prison in 1391 and remained so until 1934. Not unlike a modern concierge supplementing his income, the Palace concierge profited from vendors who leased the many shops within the Palace walls. But the prison's reality was far darker. In the 15th century, passers-by could still hear the screams of tortured prisoners in the Tour Bonbec — the most westerly tower. The name 'bon-bec' (meaning 'prate' in the Middle Ages) probably alluded to the interrogations on the ground floor: a varied spectrum of torture methods was devised to make victims confess and denounce their accomplices. During a restoration in 1828, two oubliettes were found in the tower's basement, communicating with the river and spiked with iron points — needless to dwell on the fate of the prisoners.

beats.script_body: During the Revolution, the Conciergerie boasted an impressive list of illustrious prisoners awaiting their deaths. Madame Roland, who had supported the Revolution but sided with the Girondins at the wrong time. Marie-Antoinette, who occupied a dreary cell from 2 August to 16 October 1793, when she was taken to the guillotine on Place de la Révolution. Then Danton, Robespierre and Saint-Just were detained here in their turn — Danton and Robespierre occupying the cells adjacent to the Queen's. In all, some 2,780 victims of the Revolutionary Tribunal passed through the arcade entrance to the jeers of delighted tricoteuses huddled on the perron.

beats.script_body: North of the Conciergerie's Gothic halls was a section of the prison leading to the dark cells, known as 'rue de Paris' — named after the Great Executioner, Monsieur de Paris. This post was held by seven successive generations of the Sanson family, from 1688 to 1847, transmitted from father to son. Shortly before the Revolution, Louis XVI had set his heart on improving their plight and granted Charles-Henri Sanson an annual fee of 16,000 pounds plus 2,000 crowns for the upkeep of the scaffold and pillory — never suspecting he would become his own executioner. Being a royalist, Charles-Henri had no desire to carry out that deed. On 15 August 1792 he was arrested as 'the despot's employee'; with each execution he would be dispatched from his cell to Place du Carrousel, where the guillotine stood, and afterwards taken back. When the guillotine began to work at full swing and his expert hand could not be dispensed with, he was released — but retired soon after executing his sovereign. His son Henri held the position during the Terror and beyond, until 1840. The film-maker Jean Renoir marvelled that his own grandfather — the painter's father, a tailor from Limoges — had known Henri's chief assistant during the Terror: a man who 'may have passed Voltaire and Benjamin Franklin in the street, heard Mozart play the harpsichord.' Old Renoir befriended the assistant, and as Jean Renoir observed: 'After all, they were two good workmen: one cut out cloth, the other cut off heads just as conscientiously.'

beats.script_body: At no. 115 rue Saint-Honoré stood the pharmacy where the Swedish Marshal Fersen is believed to have obtained the invisible ink for his secret correspondence with Marie-Antoinette during her sequestration at the Conciergerie. A close friend of the royal family, Fersen had tried to help them escape from France. Evidence of the existence of the pharmacy goes back to 1715, making it one of the oldest in Paris.

During the tower's restoration in 1828, workers found two oubliettes in the basement: concealed dungeons spiked with iron points and connected to the river. beats.script_body: The Conciergerie is one of the few remaining vestiges of the old medieval Palais de Justice and is Paris's oldest prison — where Marie-Antoinette and the leading figures of the Revolution were incarcerated before execution. Inside are several splendid, vaulted Gothic halls, including the Salle des Gens d'Armes, built in 1301 to 1315. The far end is separated off by an iron grille; during the Revolution this area was reserved for the pailleux, prisoners who couldn't afford to bribe a guard for their own cell and had to sleep on straw (paille).

beats.script_body: The original equestrian statue of Henry IV at the heart of the bridge was destroyed in 1792. When the Bourbons returned, the statue was rebuilt in 1818 — by public subscription. Bronze for the new statue was obtained by melting down a statue of Louis Charles Antoine Desaix. The new cast was made from a surviving mould of the original. Before the new Henri IV was sealed, the sculptor François-Frédéric Lemot hid four boxes inside it: a history of the life of Henri IV, a 17th-century parchment certifying the original statue, a document describing how the new statue had been commissioned, and a list of the people who had contributed to the public subscription.

beats.source_passage: At the point where the bridge crosses the Île de la Cité, there stands a bronze equestrian statue of king Henry IV, originally commissioned from Giambologna under the orders of Marie de Médicis, Henri's widow and Regent of France. After his death, Giambologna's assistant Pietro Tacca completed the statue, which was erected on its pedestal by Pietro Francavilla, in 1614. It was destroyed in 1792 during the French Revolution, but was rebuilt in 1818, following the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy. Commissioned from public donations, bronze for the new statue was obtained from a statue of Louis Charles Antoine Desaix and melted down. The new statue was cast from a mold made using a surviving cast of the original. Inside the statue, the new sculptor François-Frédéric Lemot put four boxes, containing a history of the life of Henry IV, a 17th-century parchment certifying the original statue, a document describing how the new statue was commissioned, and a list of people who contributed to a public subscription.

beats.script_body: The graceful, twelve-arched Pont-Neuf — despite its name, meaning New Bridge — is Paris's oldest surviving bridge. It was built by Henri IV, who is commemorated with a statue halfway across. Made of stone and free of the usual medieval complement of houses, it was a radical departure from previous structures, hence its name. Henri IV, one of the capital's first great town-planners, took much interest in the Pont-Neuf's progress and would sometimes come to inspect it, on one occasion delighting the workmen by taking a flying leap over an incomplete arch.

beats.script_body: Between 1712 and 1719, a large pump house stood on the bridge — fitted with a carillon and decorated with an image of the Samaritan woman at the well. The name stuck: La Samaritaine. The pump house was torn down in 1813. But the name lived on: years later, on the same site, the merchant Ernest Cognacq set up a stand and gradually grew his business into the department store La Samaritaine in 1869.

beats.source_passage: Between 1712 and 1719, replacing an earlier one, a large pump house was built on the bridge. It was decorated with an image of the Samaritan woman at the well. As a result, the structure (which included a carillon) was named La Samaritaine. Years after it was torn down (in 1813), Ernest Cognacq, a 19th-century merchant, set up a stand on the site and gradually grew his business to what became, in 1869, the department store La Samaritaine.

beats.script_body: The picturesque green bookstalls of the bouquinistes along the quais are a remnant of the days when the Pont-Neuf was a world of its own, crowded with strollers, pedlars, acrobats, prostitutes, and riff-raff. When the bridge was cleaned up in the late 18th century, its hucksters spilled over to the quais and eventually settled into the book trade.

beats.script_body: Louis Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of the Boulevard du Temple is the picture usually called the first photograph in which a human being can be seen. But two years earlier, between 1836 and 1837, Daguerre was running outdoor tests of his new technique — and one of those tests pointed at the Pont Neuf. It captured the bridge and the equestrian statue of Henry IV. On the lower-left of the image, in the shadow of the statue, what appears to be a worker — perhaps two — can be seen lying against the fence. If the dating holds, that figure may be the first human ever photographed.

beats.source_passage: In 1838, Louis Daguerre produced his famous daguerreotype portrait of the View of the Boulevard du Temple, widely considered the first photograph where a human can be seen. However, between 1836 and 1837, Daguerre made several tests, in order to experiment with and perfect the new technique in an outdoor environment. One surviving example is an image of the Pont Neuf and the equestrian statue of Henry IV, made possibly as early as 1836. On the lower-left side of the image, what appears to be a worker, or perhaps two, can be seen lying against the fence, in the shadow of the statue.

beats.script_body: So impressive was the bridge in scale and length that it soon became symbolic of the city itself, drawing large crowds. Pedlars, secondhand book- and flower-sellers, dog-barbers and tooth-pullers set up stalls, while acrobats and actors entertained passers-by.

beats.script_body: Three hundred and eighty-one carved stone faces decorate the bridge — each one different from the others. They are heads of forest and field divinities from ancient mythology, plus satyrs and sylvains, copies of originals attributed to the French Renaissance sculptor Germain Pilon — who also carved the tomb of Henry II and Catherine de'Medici at Saint-Denis. The Pilon originals lasted until 1851-1854, when the bridge was completely rebuilt. Six were sent to the Musée Carnavalet, eight others to the Cluny — they are now at the Musée National de la Renaissance at Château d'Écouen. The new copies were carved by Hippolyte Maindron, Hubert Lavigne, Antoine-Louis Barye and Fontenelle — Fontenelle alone made 61, on the upstream side between the right bank and the Île de la Cité.

beats.source_passage: The mascarons are 381 stone masks, each different from the others, which decorate the sides of the bridge. They represent the heads of forest and field divinities from ancient mythology, as well as satyrs and sylvains. They are copies of the originals attributed to the French Renaissance sculptor Germain Pilon (1525–1590), who also sculpted the tomb of King Henry II of France and Queen Catherine de'Medici in the Basilica of St Denis, five kilometers north of Paris. The mascarons remained in place until 1851–1854, when the bridge was completely rebuilt. At that time six of the original mascarons from the 16th century were placed in the Musée Carnavalet, along with eight molds of other originals. Eight other originals were first placed in the Musée de Cluny – Musée national du Moyen Âge, and are now in the French National Museum of the Renaissance in the Château d'Écouen. During their reconstruction, the Renaissance masks were replaced with copies made by noted 19th-century sculptors, including Hippolyte Maindron, Hubert Lavigne, Antoine-Louis Barye and Fontenelle. Fontenelle made 61 masks, which are found on the upstream side of the bridge between the right bank and the Île de la Cité.

poi.name: Hotel de Ville
poi.short_description: Neo-Renaissance Paris City Hall that served as Revolution headquarters where Robespierre was arrested in 1794

beats.script_body: Place de Greve hosted the fete de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, when a 10-metre-high bonfire celebrated the birth of John the Baptist. Occasionally the King himself would come to light the fire, heralded by trumpets.

The anti-bourgeois proletarian Commune burnt down the Hotel de Ville in 1871. The victorious bourgeois government of the Third Republic rebuilt it at once in its old style, to brush off this incident and demonstrate that its possession was irrevocable.

The municipality of Paris grew from the corporation of water merchants who bought the strand (greve) from Louis VII in the 12th century. A tribunal of commerce was set up on Place de Greve, becoming the embryo of the municipality. The corporation's seal, inherited from the ancient Nautae Parisiaci, remains the coat of arms of Paris with only minor changes a thousand years later.

Etienne Marcel, provost of Paris, was the first to settle the city government in a town hall on Place de Greve, buying a two-storeyed house from the king on behalf of the city in 1357. Known as La Maison des Piliers for its row of arcades, it was eventually replaced by a magnificent Renaissance building begun under Francois I.

After the Commune burned the original Hotel de Ville in 1871, the Third Republic rebuilt it with lavish interiors designed to project the permanence and grandeur of the new regime. Inside you'll find a bust by Rodin and magnificent murals by Puvis de Chavannes — some of the finest civic decorations in Paris.

Place de Greve was where people gathered in early morning to seek work, a practice called 'faire la greve.' The expression survives in modern French but now means 'to go on strike' — the opposite of its original meaning of seeking employment.

On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sevigne watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers carried to Place de Greve. The Marquise had poisoned her father (requiring ten attempts) and two brothers. Her lover Godin de Sainte-Croix had learned the art of poison from an Italian named Exili while imprisoned in the Bastille. Sevigne wrote: 'At last, it is all over, the Brinvilliers is in the air.'

Place de Greve served as Paris's main place of public executions, with gallows as a permanent fixture. Notable executions included Cartouche, the terror of early 18th-century Paris; Ravaillac, assassin of Henri IV; and the Marquise de Brinvilliers, mass poisoner.
